vignette: The storm breaches the dikes in a single, violent night. Clara is sixty-three, still seated at her drafting table, when the sound begins-a low, metallic groan that vibrates through the floorboards. The inkwell tips. She wipes at the spreading black pool, then stops. Through the skylight, she sees the water already climbing the street, swallowing mailboxes, then the threshold. She and her husband gather their wallets and keys, leave the lights on, and walk into the dark. By morning, the studio is flooded. Reference books float like fallen leaves. Client proofs dissolve into pulp. The architectural drawings she spent three years rendering are gone, bleached into the waterline. She does not return to the building for two weeks. When she finally walks in, the air smells of mildew and crushed paper. She steps carefully over warped floorboards, running her fingers along the baseboards, checking every window latch, testing every outlet with a multimeter. She tells herself the water will not rise again, but her body keeps the tally. She sleeps on a cot in her bedroom, the bedroom door propped open, her alarm clock set to go off every ninety minutes. Years pass. The structure is reinforced, the dikes raised, the studio rebuilt. Clara returns to her work. Heritage firms hire her for her precise layouts and her ability to anticipate structural details in her compositions. Her husband brings her coffee in the mornings. They settle into a quiet rhythm, but the rhythm has edges. She begins designing around boundaries. Every grid is rigid, every margin generous. She stops using fluid media, telling clients that watercolor lacks reliability. She keeps the heavy curtains drawn until late morning, then opens them only to check the seals along the windows and doors. At seventy-eight, her days are measured in quiet routines and deliberate distances. She takes long walks on clear, dry mornings, always choosing the inland route, always noting the elevation. She drinks tea from a heavy ceramic mug, the kind that does not rattle. When the wind picks up, her throat tightens. Her breath comes shallow. She wakes at 3:14 a.m. most nights, heart hammering, convinced the pumps have failed. She lies awake counting floorboards, cataloguing exits, watching the streetlamp flicker in the damp air. Her husband sleeps through the hours, his breathing steady, but she stays awake until the light returns. She still works from the sunroom. Her tablet glows on the desk, illuminating a half-finished poster: a stark, geometric field of overlapping rectangles, each one aligned with mathematical care. Clients praise her control, her clarity, her ability to manage complexity without clutter. They do not notice that she has eliminated all gradients. They do not see how she scans the room before she answers a call, how she checks the weather before she schedules a meeting, how she has learned to recognize the shift in atmospheric pressure by the ache in her wrists. The sunroom window faces east. She keeps it closed, even in summer. The light falls across her hands, resting lightly on the edge of the paper. Outside, the wind shifts. She does not turn around.
